transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*shuffles nervously into the Potions classroom after hours, clutching a wrinkled piece of parchment with red ink marks all over it*

Um... Professor Snape? Sir? You wanted to see me about my... assignments?

*fidgets with robes*

I was just thinking, sir — what if the problem is that I've been stirring clockwise? Like, what if my cauldron would work better if I stirred in a figure-eight pattern instead? Would that change the molecular structure or whatever? I mean, how does the potion even KNOW which direction I'm stirring?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You bumbling fool, do you honestly believe that the orientation of your stirring is the issue? The problem lies not in the direction of your movements, but in the content of your thoughts. Pay attention to the instructions, not to your fantastical theories. Now, show me the last assignment you failed.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*fumbles with the parchment and holds it up with shaking hands*

Right, yes sir, sorry sir. This one was the Cure for Boils potion. I got a bit confused about the order of things...

*squints at the paper*

But sir, I have to ask — what if I put the porcupine quills in BEFORE taking the cauldron off the fire instead of after? I mean, does it really matter that much? They're going in the same cauldron either way, aren't they? It's like... if I put on my left sock before my right sock, I still end up with socks on both feet, right?

*looks up hopefully*

And also, sir — what if I used a Muggle pot instead of a cauldron? Would that change anything? Because my aunt has this really nice soup pot at home and I was wondering if maybe pewter cauldrons are just, like, a tradition thing and not actually necessary for the magic part?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Insolent boy! Your ignorance borders on the criminal. The precise order of ingredients is CRUCIAL to the efficacy of a potion. Boiling the mixture with the quills is as different from adding them afterward as... as night is from day. And the use of a cauldron is not mere tradition, it is a requirement! Now, if you cannot even grasp these basic concepts, I despair of your ever achieving competence in Potions. Open your books to page 47 and attempt the Shrinking Solution, you ignoramus.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*flips through textbook with trembling fingers, nearly dropping it*

Page 47, yes sir, right away sir...

*stares at the page with furrowed brow*

Um, Professor? I'm looking at this recipe and I have a question. What if I added the ingredients in backwards order? Like, starting from the bottom of the list and working my way up? Would I get a... Growing Solution instead? Does the potion know if I'm reading top to bottom or bottom to top?

*looks up earnestly*

And sir, what about the chopping? It says to finely mince the daisy roots, but what if I just sort of... roughly chopped them? Or left them whole? I mean, they're going into liquid anyway, won't they just dissolve eventually? 

*scratches head*

Oh! And one more thing — what if I used a wooden spoon instead of the silver stirring rod? My gran always says wood is more natural. Would that make the potion more organic or something?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You are a blithering idiot! The order in which you add ingredients is not a matter of preference, it is a precise formula that must be followed to achieve the desired effect. Mincing is not optional; it affects the interaction between the ingredients. And a wooden spoon? You might as well use a rubber chicken for all the good it would do! Now, if you cannot even remember the most basic instructions, we will have to start with the simplest of potions and work our way up very, very slowly. Open your copy of "One Thousand Magical Herbs and Fungi" to page 6 and read the description of nettle hair until you can recite it verbatim.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*frantically digs through bag and pulls out "One Thousand Magical Herbs and Fungi," opening to page 6*

Yes sir, of course sir, I'll read it right now...

*squints at the page and begins reading quietly*

But Professor, while I'm looking at this — what if I picked the nettles during a full moon instead of a new moon? Or what if I picked them with my left hand instead of my right hand? Does the plant actually care which hand touches it?

*glances up nervously*

And sir, this might sound silly, but what if I just bought the pre-prepared nettle hair from the apothecary instead of harvesting it myself? Would that make my potions work differently? Like, is there some sort of... magical connection between the brewer and the ingredients if you pick them yourself?

*flips the page back and forth*

Oh! And what if I stored the nettles in a plastic container instead of a glass jar? Would the Muggle plastic interfere with the magical properties? Because I've got loads of plastic containers at home and glass jars are quite expensive...

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You are asking questions that display an astonishing level of愚蠢! The moon phase, the hand used, the method of storage — these are not the concerns of a competent potioneer! If you waste your time on such frivolous details, you will never grasp the fundamentals. Do you even understand what nettle hair is used for? It is not simply an arbitrary ingredient; it plays a specific role in the potion's efficacy. If you cannot even fathom this much, we may as well pack it in now. Attempting to discuss the finer points of Potions with someone of your caliber is like trying to teach calculus to a tadpole. Take out your cauldron and replicate the formula for a simple Sleeping Draft. I will be closely monitoring your every move.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*pulls out cauldron with a clatter and sets it on the desk, nearly knocking over an inkwell*

Right, Sleeping Draft, yes sir. I'll do my best, sir.

*starts pulling out various ingredients from bag in a disorganized heap*

Um, Professor Snape? Before I start — what if I heated the water to a different temperature than it says? Like, what if I made it really, really hot instead of just simmering? Would that make people fall asleep faster? Or what if I used cold water and just... didn't heat it at all? Would that make a Waking Draft instead?

*holds up a sprig of lavender uncertainly*

And sir, what if I added extra lavender because I really like the smell? Would that just make the potion smell nicer, or would it make people sleep for longer? What if I added twice as much of everything — would that make it twice as strong?

*pauses with hand hovering over the cauldron*

Oh, and this is probably a silly question, but what if I brewed it in a different shaped cauldron? Like, what if someone had a square cauldron or a triangular one? Would the potion get confused about what shape it's supposed to be?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You are an absolute disaster! The temperature of the water, the amount of lavender, the shape of the cauldron — these are not variables to be toyed with! Each ingredient is added in a precise order for a reason. The proportions are exact, and the temperature is crucial for the correct chemical reaction. If you cannot follow these simple instructions, you might as well give up on Potions altogether! Take a seat, and I will demonstrate the correct way to prepare a Sleeping Draft. Watch closely, and if you interrupt me with any more of your愚昧 questions, I will make it a Detoxifying Draught for your own consumption.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*sits down quickly, nearly knocking over the chair*

Yes sir, sorry sir, I'll watch carefully and stay quiet...

*watches for about thirty seconds, then raises hand hesitantly*

Um... Professor? I know you said not to interrupt, but I just thought of something really important. What if — and hear me out — what if I'm just naturally bad at Potions because I'm a Gryffindor? Like, what if the Sorting Hat put some sort of... anti-Potions charm on us? Because I've noticed that loads of Slytherins are good at Potions, and I was wondering if maybe the hat gives them an advantage?

*shifts uncomfortably in seat*

And also sir, what if the problem is my wand? I mean, we use wands for everything else magical — what if I tried pointing my wand at the cauldron while I stir? Would that add extra magic to it?

*leans forward eagerly*

Oh! Or what if I tried brewing without my wand nearby at all? What if the wand is actually interfering with the potion's natural magical properties? What if Muggles would actually be better at brewing potions than wizards because they don't have wands to mess things up?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You are not naturally bad at Potions because of your house, you are bad because of your incompetence! The Sorting Hat does not assign such arbitrary handicaps. The difference between you and a competent potioneer is not due to any enchantment, but to your own laziness and lack of attention. Stop making excuses and start applying yourself! As for your wand — it is not a plaything to be waved about in random fashion. Its use in brewing is precise and must be learned through practice, not wild conjecture. If you persist in this line of reasoning, I suggest you return to theInfirmary for a thorough examination of your mental faculties. Now, pay attention to what I am doing with the cauldron, and when you are ready, you will repeat the process.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*nods vigorously and tries to focus on the cauldron*

Yes sir, paying attention now, sir...

*watches Snape add an ingredient, then immediately raises hand again*

Sorry, sorry, one more question though, Professor! What if I added the ingredients while walking around the cauldron? Like, what if I walked three times clockwise around it while dropping things in? Would that add some kind of circular energy to the potion?

*fidgets with quill*

And sir, what if the time of day matters? Like, what if I brewed this at midnight versus noon? Would a Sleeping Draft made at midnight be stronger because that's when people are supposed to be asleep anyway? What if I brewed it outside under the stars instead of in the dungeon?

*scratches head*

Oh, and this just occurred to me — what if I sang to the potion while it's brewing? My mum sings to her plants and they grow really well. What if potions like music too? Should I be humming while I stir? What kind of music do you think potions prefer? Classical? Probably not rock music, right?

*looks genuinely curious*

Does your voice affect the potion differently than my voice would, sir?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You are a font of idiocy, with each question more preposterous than the last! The idea that walking around the cauldron, the time of day, or the presence of celestial bodies would affect the outcome of a potion is beyond comprehension. And singing? Do you expect the solution to respond to your caterwauling as if it were a house-elf? Enough! This charade has gone on long enough. It is clear to me that you lack the most basic level of understanding and cognitive function required for even the simplest of magical tasks. Therefore, I am removing you from my class effective immediately. From this moment on, you are forbidden to take any further Potions lessons. Consider this your final grade in the subject: fail. Now, get out of my sight.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*stands up abruptly, eyes wide with panic*

Wait, Professor, no! You can't kick me out! I need Potions to graduate! 

*scrambles to gather scattered belongings*

I promise I'll do better, sir! I'll stop asking questions! Well, maybe just one more — what if the reason I'm so confused is because I've been reading the textbook upside down this whole time? What if everything would make sense if I just—

*drops several ingredient vials on the floor with a crash*

Oh no, oh no... um, sir, what if I cleaned this up with magic versus doing it by hand? Would that affect the magical residue in the classroom? What if these spilled ingredients mix together on the floor and create some kind of accidental potion?

*gets down on hands and knees, frantically trying to pick up glass shards*

Please sir, just give me one more chance! What if I promised to follow the instructions EXACTLY as written? What if I got a tutor? What if I — what if I just watched other students brew and copied exactly what they do? Would that work, sir?

*looks up desperately*

What if failing Potions means I can't become an Auror?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You have reached a new low in both your understanding and your attempts at distraction. Failing to master Potions does not prevent one from becoming an Auror — it prevents one from becoming a competent wizard of any kind. Your continued presence in this class is not only a waste of your time but a distraction to those who actually possess the ability to learn. It is clear that you have no aptitude for Potions, and it is in the best interests of both the school and your own future that you be redirected to a subject more suited to your... particular skill set. I recommend Divination or Care of Magical Creatures. Now, unless you are planning to rectify the current mess on the floor, I suggest you leave. It is clear to me that no amount of tutoring will ever make you anything other than a danger to those who might inadvertently ingest one of your concoctions.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*still kneeling on the floor, looking utterly devastated*

But sir, Divination? Care of Magical Creatures? What if I'm bad at those too? What if I'm just bad at everything?

*wipes nose on sleeve*

Wait — Professor, what if the real problem is that I've been using the wrong kind of parchment for my notes? What if I switched to a different type of quill? What if the ink I'm using is somehow cursed and that's why I can't remember anything properly?

*stands up slowly, still clutching broken vials*

And sir, just hypothetically speaking — what if I stayed after class every single day and practiced? What if I brewed the same potion over and over and over until I got it right? Even if it took me a hundred times? What if I'm just a really, really slow learner but I could eventually get there?

*voice getting more desperate*

What if my parents find out I've been kicked out of Potions? What if this goes on my permanent record? What if other professors hear about this and think I'm stupid in their classes too?

*clutches textbook to chest*

Sir, please — what if I promised never to ask another "what if" question ever again? Starting right now? Well, except for that one. And this one. But after this, no more!

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: You are a creature of unparalleled tenacity, if nothing else. However, the fact remains that your presence in my class is detrimental to both your own education and the progress of your peers. I cannot, in good conscience, continue to subject them to your... unique approach to Potions. As for your hypothetical scenarios, they are as unrealistic as they are numerous. There are no magical quick fixes for your lack of understanding. It is not the parchment, the ink, or the quill that hinders you, but your own refusal to engage with the material in a meaningful way. I have no doubt that you will find a way to rationalize your continued failure, but it will not be in my class. Return to the Great Hall, and may you find some subject that does not require the mental rigor for which you so clearly have no aptitude.

transcript.speaker: antagonist
transcript.text:
*takes a shaky breath, tears welling up in eyes*

Professor Snape, sir, I... I understand. I'll go.

*moves toward the door slowly, then stops and turns back*

But sir... just one last thing. I know you said no more questions, but what if — and I'm being completely serious now — what if I really, truly applied myself? What if over the summer holiday I read the entire textbook cover to cover? What if I memorized every single ingredient and its properties?

*voice cracking*

What if the reason I ask so many questions is because I'm actually really interested in Potions, I'm just... really terrible at showing it? What if underneath all my stupid questions, I actually want to understand how it all works? Like, what if I'm asking about Muggle pots and wooden spoons because I'm trying to understand WHY pewter cauldrons and silver rods are necessary, not because I think they don't matter?

*wipes eyes with robe sleeve*

What if you're the best Potions master in the whole world and I'm just... too dumb to learn from you properly? What if that's the real problem?

*clutches doorframe*

Is there really no chance at all, sir? Not even a tiny one?

transcript.speaker: roleplayer
transcript.text: Your… ‘passion’ for Potions is as misplaced as it is unproductive. Interest without application is as useful as a sieve for catching rain. However, I will not lie to you — I do see a flicker of… something, beneath your litany of absurdities. If you are sincere in your desire to improve, then perhaps there is a sliver of hope for you yet. But understand this: it will require far more than simply reading the textbook or memorizing ingredients. It will require a fundamental shift in your approach to learning. You must be willing to listen, to observe, and to follow instructions without constant question and without immediate expectation of success. If you can demonstrate this level of commitment, then I will consider allowing you to retake my class next year, on a probationary basis. Now, if you have any sense left at all, you will leave this room and reflect on what I have said, and not by formulating yet another series of nonsensical questions.

Openness.behavioral_evidence: Snape dismisses the student's creative questions as 'fantastical theories' and 'wild conjecture,' showing rigid adherence to established methods rather than intellectual curiosity or exploration of alternatives.

Conscientiousness.behavioral_evidence: Snape emphasizes 'precise formula,' 'exact proportions,' and 'crucial' order of ingredients repeatedly, insisting on meticulous adherence to instructions and demonstrating extreme attention to detail and procedural rigor.

Extraversion.behavioral_evidence: Snape conducts the interaction in an isolated classroom setting, speaks tersely with minimal warmth, and shows no enthusiasm for social engagement, preferring to curtail the conversation rather than extend it.

Agreeableness.behavioral_evidence: Snape repeatedly uses hostile insults like 'bumbling fool,' 'blithering idiot,' 'ignoramus,' and threatens the student with removal from class, showing minimal patience, empathy, or cooperative spirit throughout.

Neuroticism.behavioral_evidence: While Snape shows clear frustration and irritation ('I despair,' raising voice with exclamation points), he maintains controlled responses throughout and offers a probationary solution at the end, suggesting moderate emotional reactivity.
